articles.title: This new Google Earth feature will change how you explore the world
articles.excerpt: Your favorite places just became the canvas for your biggest ideas.
articles.body: TL;DR Google Earth now uses Gemini’s Nano Banana 2 to generate AI images based on real-world locations using satellite, aerial, and 3D map data. You can visualize ideas or learn about places by creating concept images, redesigning public spaces, or generating easy-to-read historical infographics for landmarks. The feature is rolling out globally today for Google Earth on the web, letting users turn real locations into AI-powered visual concepts with a simple text prompt. Google Earth has always been great for showing you what’s already there. Now, Google wants it to help you imagine what could be there instead. The company is bringing Gemini’s Nano Banana 2 image generation model to Google Earth on the web, letting you create AI-generated images based on real locations.

articles.title: Your Agent's Memory Is a Markdown File. Let's Audit It.
articles.excerpt: Quick check: does your agent stack have a memory.md in it somewhere? An AGENTS.md? A notes file the agent appends to when something seems worth keeping? Thought so. Mine did too. It's the pattern ever…
articles.body: Quick check: does your agent stack have a memory.md in it somewhere? An AGENTS.md ? A notes file the agent appends to when something seems worth keeping? Thought so. Mine did too. It's the pattern everyone converges on, it takes twenty minutes to build, and it genuinely works — right up until the day it hands a customer a fact that stopped being true in March. This post does three things: shows you exactly why the pattern rots (with a real-shaped sample file we'll dissect), gives you a small script to audit your own file tonight, and walks through the architecture change that actually fixes it. No vendor required for any of it.

articles.title: The 300px Canvas Bug That Shrunk My React Image Editor
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for DEV's Summer Bug Smash: Clear the Lineup powered by Sentry. I am building a browser-based text removal workspace where a user uploads an image, paints over unwanted text or ob…
articles.body: This is a submission for DEV's Summer Bug Smash: Clear the Lineup powered by Sentry . Project Overview I am building a browser-based text removal workspace where a user uploads an image, paints over unwanted text or objects, and sends the resulting mask to an image-editing pipeline. The mask editor uses three stacked <canvas> elements: a base canvas for the uploaded image; an overlay canvas for the painted mask; a cursor canvas for the brush preview and pointer events. All three canvases must have identical dimensions. The pointer coordinates must also map back to the same bitmap coordinate system, or the generated mask will not match the part of the image the user selected.

articles.title: Emergent Design & Gall's Law: When Complex Coding Problems Dissolve Instead of Being Solved
articles.excerpt: I recently read an article by the main maintainer of InversifyJS describing the journey of rebuilding its dependency resolution algorithm. What caught my attention wasn't the performance improvements…
articles.body: I recently read an article by the main maintainer of InversifyJS describing the journey of rebuilding its dependency resolution algorithm . What caught my attention wasn't the performance improvements or the technical details. It was something much more familiar. As I was reading, I realized they were experiencing the exact same phenomenon I had experienced years ago while creating InversifyJS. It reminded me of something that, until now, I had never really put into words. The temptation to solve the hardest problem first Every engineer has experienced it. You're implementing a feature when you encounter a design problem that feels wrong. You know the current approach won't scale, and you know there must be a beautiful abstraction somewhere, so you stop writing code and start designing.

articles.title: How to store AI-generated images per user in object storage and delete the old ones
articles.excerpt: Use one key prefix per user, delete from the application every key you can name, and leave lifecycle rules to sweep the old temporary images nobody will ever ask for again. That's the whole design, an…
articles.body: Use one key prefix per user, delete from the application every key you can name, and leave lifecycle rules to sweep the old temporary images nobody will ever ask for again. That's the whole design, and I've watched teams get it wrong in the same two ways for years: they either try to make the storage layer clever enough to know what a user is, or they hand the entire deletion problem to a lifecycle policy and then wonder why an account-deletion request took nine days to actually remove anything. I design data layers for a living, so I'm going to be blunt about the durability and consistency side of this rather than the upload-a-file-in-five-minutes side. Why the key layout matters more than the backend you pick Object storage has no folders.

articles.title: The most important sci-fi movie of the century is about to leave Netflix
articles.excerpt: 12 years later, Alex Garland's directorial debut still holds up
articles.body: It’s tough to picture it now, but AI used to be the stuff of science fiction . Ever since the ‘60s, the topic has been fertile ground for inspiration, resulting in memorable creations, from the evil HAL in 2001: A Space Odyssey to the pity-inducing replicants of Blade Runner . While these movies remain classics, we’re in an era of AI that might reshape the way the technology is depicted in fiction. Instead of visualizing it as something far off and ripe for exploring, we’re encountering it in our daily lives. Your opinions on AI may vary, but one thing is clear: It’s a far less sexy topic than what was promised.

articles.title: A SpaceX rocket will crash into the moon next week, and scientists aren't sure what to expect
articles.excerpt: Scientists are preparing to study the effects of human-made impacts on the moon when a spent SpaceX rocket stage impacts the lunar surface on Aug. 5.
articles.body: On Aug. 5, Earth's moon is due for a human-made, high-speed impact from an identified flying object: a spent SpaceX Falcon 9 upper stage. The event will lead to a literal "dust up" on the lunar landscape. That Falcon 9 upper stage is a leftover from the launch that sent Firefly's Blue Ghost-1 lander to the moon on Jan. 15, 2025. Onboard the same flight was the Hakuto-R Mission 2 , called Resilience, a robotic lunar lander developed by the Japanese company ispace. And according to a new study by an international team published on the open-source arXiv server, the resulting impact plume may briefly be bright enough to see against the dark sky near the moon's edge. That means it might be visible to moongazers with sufficiently sensitive telescopes.

articles.title: The Defiant is a Story-Driven Shooter that Explores a Rarely Seen Side of WW2 | IGN Preview
articles.excerpt: Hands-on impressions of this gritty new singleplayer shooter set during the Second Sino-Japanese War.
articles.body: From the D-Day landing that opened Medal of Honor: Frontline to the Battle of the Bulge that capped off the American campaign in the original Call of Duty, it feels like videogames have already told and retold most of the major conflicts that occurred during the second world war. However, while players have previously stepped into the combat boots of soldiers on the ground in various settings from Sicily to Stalingrad, the events of China’s War of Resistance against the Japanese invasion have largely been overlooked. That’s where The Defiant comes in. This story-driven singleplayer shooter from developer Hangzhou Hoothanes Entertainment is set to explore the prolonged and devastating conflict from the perspective of multiple Chinese soldiers.

articles.title: Project Motor Racing Adds Free Holden Commodore, PC Triple-Screen Support in 2.1 Update
articles.excerpt: New, free V8 Supercars DLC pack launches alongside a “significant new update” for Project Motor Racing, which includes a total rebuild of the handling model for the GT3 and GT4 categories.
articles.body: Giants Software and Straight4 Studios have launched a new, free DLC pack alongside a “significant new update” for Project Motor Racing. Update 2.1 includes a total rebuild of the handling model for the GT3 and GT4 categories, Alpha triple-screen support on PC, and more. The ‘Aussie Rivals’ pack brings one of the greatest rivalries in motorsport to Project Motor Racing for the first time, introducing the 2013 Holden VF Commodore and a “completely reworked” 2013 Ford Falcon FG. These Australian domestic models represented the last truly local clash between Holden and Ford, before Holden transitioned to the imported ZB Commodore shell in 2018 and the death of car manufacturing in Australia saw the Supercars series subsequently shift to Chevrolet Camaro and Ford Mustang shells.
